title: How to avoid hamstring pulls during deadlifts
summary: NH argues that hamstring pulls on deadlifts happen because the deadlift trains hamstrings only in the positive, and many lifters never train their eccentric lengthening. Keep deadlifting positive-only but add higher-rep lengthening movements like RDLs, back extensions and good mornings, while being cautious with unforgiving lifts such as Nordic curls and some glute-ham raises.
claims: Hamstring pulls are nearly 100% avoidable, outside of predisposition or technique issues
People pull hamstrings on the positive portion of the deadlift, never the negative
When a lift opens with the positive, the negative tends to be rushed or ignored
The deadlift trains the hamstrings only in the positive; for many lifters it and its variations are their only hamstring stimulus
Every other muscle is trained through both negative and positive; the hamstrings are often the exception
Paused deadlifts, stiff-leg deadlifts and rack pulls are great but still do not train hamstring lengthening
Hamstring pulls happen when the bar stalls or dips and the lifter grinds, causing a quick lengthen-then-contract the unprepared hamstring cannot handle
Do not start doing slow negatives on the deadlift; it would tire you and sandbag the positive you want to progress
Add hip-hinge or hamstring movements that lengthen the hamstring under control
A lifter who only did pin bench for years, letting the bar drop, would risk injury trying a slow negative because the muscles are unprepared for it
A negative that is not resisted, where gravity does the work, does not count as a negative
Train hamstring lengthening at higher reps in lower intensity windows; it both conditions against injury and adds hypertrophy
Best hamstring lengthening lifts are Romanian deadlifts, back hyperextensions and good mornings
On good mornings, use the lower back as a bridge, not a crane, to avoid lower-back pain
Some glute-ham raise variations and Nordic curls can create uncontrolled stretches where the hamstring is the only thing that can snap, especially for heavy lifters new to them
The most dangerous lifts are those with no safe way out on failure, like good mornings, which still force extra lumbar flexion even with safeties
Keep high intensity for the deadlift and do unforgiving hamstring movements in lower intensity windows
The deadlift is a very safe lift if done with proper technique
Adding lengthening work improves mobility over time, but rehab takes patience with weight selection and frequency
Training only the positive or only the negative of any movement pattern sets you up for trouble
You do not need foam rolling to prevent hamstring pulls; complement training with negatives
Hamstring pulls are rarely a technique problem; technique matters more for lower-back injuries
exercises: keep it positive-only; don't add slow negatives
progress the positive; safe with good technique
use lower back as a bridge not a crane; be careful with stretch
hamstring lengthening; no way out on failure
some variations are extreme; use caution
